description: Scottish landscapes and later geological investigations trace water, deep time, mountain building, glaciation and the dependence of life on energy from the Sun.

s04e01.description: Stewart traces how Scotland’s rivers, lochs and rainfall were reshaped by reservoirs, hydroelectric schemes and other engineering, turning the country’s water into one of its most heavily managed natural systems.

s04e02.description: The story of James Hutton shows how observations of Scottish rock overturned short biblical timescales and established the concept of deep geological time at the foundation of modern geology.

s04e03.description: Stewart follows Edward Bailey’s evidence that Scotland once contained immense volcanoes and the work of Arthur Holmes, whose ideas helped explain how Earth’s crust and mountains move.

s04e04.description: Louis Agassiz’s ice-age theory and James Croll’s orbital calculations reveal how nineteenth-century investigators learned that glaciers repeatedly transformed Scotland and that climate follows long natural cycles.

s04e05.description: Plants’ ability to capture sunlight is shown as a planetary revolution that oxygenated the atmosphere, reshaped ecosystems and drove evolutionary contests from ancient forests to the age of dinosaurs.
